Manuel's answers to the first grilling round on this ticket, 2026-09-30, kept word for word. The round's questions are summarized in one line each so the answers read in context; the research behind them is [wording-and-reader-context.md](https://github.com/Zenoctra/factory918/blob/research/wording-and-reader-context/docs/research/wording-and-reader-context.md).

**Q1, what makes a rule one the reader may not overrule?** Claude proposed that it takes both: the rule states the task itself (what's wanted, what done means, what isn't the reader's to decide) rather than how to get there, and its owner said it must be followed.

> (c) Ill be honest, this got a little abstract for me to track. But as much as I could, C seems like a good answer, but if I need a more intuitive understanding of what that looks like in practice to answer future questions, we are gonna have to slow down and explain it to me again in a different way.

**Q2, how is what the writer knows about the route written down?** Claude proposed: as a resource with its reason, never as an order; context given generously, method sparingly.

> (b) Also, on the 3rd note you mentioned about the number of rules increasing leading to fewer and fewer being followed as focus is split. This is a pretty big detail that I already knew but it's worth pinning for keeping in mind with all decisions as well as maybe future planning, but some things that help include heavy co-related terms.
